source_text: Τί οὖν φαμεν; Ὅτι, πρὸς ἕτερα βλέποντος τοῦ Ἀποστόλου, καὶ τὰς ψυχὰς ἡμῶν πειρωμένου χαμόθεν πρὸς ὕψος μετεωρίζειν, καὶ ἐπὶ τὸ οὐράνιον μετατιθέναι πολίτευμα, οἱ μὴ ἐφικνούμενοι τῆς μεγαλονοίας τοῦ νομοθέτου, περὶ γῆν καὶ σάρκας, ὡς περὶ τέλμα σκώληκες, ἰλυσπώ μενοι ἐν τοῖς τοῦ σώματος πάθεσι, τὸ δυνατὸν τῶν ἀποστολικῶν διατάξεων ἀπαιτοῦσιν. Ὁ δὲ προκαλεῖται εἰς τὸ πάντοτε χαίρειν οὐχὶ τὸν τυχόντα, ἀλλὰ τὸν οἷος αὐτὸς ἦν, οὐκέτι ζῶν ἐν σαρκὶ, ἀλλὰ ζῶντα ἔχων ἐν ἑαυτῷ τὸν Χριστὸν, ὡς τῆς πρὸς τὸ ἀκρότατον τῶν ἀγαθῶν συναφείας μηδαμῶς τὴν ἀπὸ τῶν ὀχληρῶν τῆς σαρκὸς συμπάθειαν δεχομένης. Ἀλλὰ κἂν διακόπτηται ἡ σὰρξ, ἡ τῆς συνεχείας διάλυσις ἐναπομένει τῷ πεπονθότι τοῦ σώματος μέρει, τῆς διαδόσεως τοῦ λυποῦντος οὐ δυναμέ νης διικνεῖσθαι πρὸς τὸ νοερὸν τῆς ψυχῆς. Εἰ γὰρ ἐνεκρώσαμεν τὰ μέλη τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς, κατὰ τὰς ὑποθήκας τοῦ Ἀποστόλου, καὶ τὴν νέκρωσιν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἐν τῷ σώματι περιεφέρομεν, ἀναγκαίως ἡ ἀπὸ τοῦ νενεκρωμένου σώματος πληγὴ πρὸς τὴν ἀπολελυμένην τῆς συναφείας αὐτοῦ ψυχὴν οὐ χωρή σει. Ἀτιμίαι δὲ καὶ ζημίαι, καὶ οἰκείων θάνατοι οὐκ ἀναβήσονται πρὸς τὸν νοῦν, οὐδὲ καταστρέψουσι τὸ ὑψηλὸν τῆς ψυχῆς πρὸς τὴν ὧδε συμπάθειαν. Εἰ μὲν γὰρ τὰ αὐτὰ φρονοῦσι τῷ σπουδαίῳ οἱ ταῖς δυσκολίαις περιπεσόντες, οὐ παρέξουσι λύπας ἑτέρῳ, οἵ γε μηδ' αὐτοὶ λυπηρῶς διαφέροντες τὰ συμπίπτοντα· εἰ δὲ κατὰ σάρκα ζῶσιν, οὐδ' οὕτω λυπή σουσιν, ἀλλ' ἐλεεινοὶ κριθήσονται, οὐ τῶν περι στάσεων μᾶλλον, ἢ τοῦ μὴ προαιρεῖσθαι τὰ δέοντα. Ὅλως δὲ ψυχὴ, ἡ ἅπαξ προσδεθεῖσα τῷ πόθῳ τοῦ Κτίσαντος, καὶ τοῖς ἐκεῖ κάλλεσιν ἐνειθισμένη φαιδρύνεσθαι, τὸ περιχαρὲς αὐτῆς καὶ εὔθυμον ὑπὸ τῆς ποικίλης μεταπτώσεως τῶν σαρκικῶν παθημά των οὐ μεταβαλεῖ· ἀλλὰ τὰ τοῖς ἄλλοις λυπηρὰ προσ θήκην εὐφροσύνης ποιήσεται. Οἷος ἦν ὁ Ἀπόστολος, εὐδοκῶν ἐν ἀσθενείαις, ἐν θλίψεσιν, ἐν διωγμοῖς, ἐν ἀνάγκαις, καυχήματα ἑαυτοῦ τὰς ἐνδείας ποιούμενος· ἐν λιμῷ καὶ δίψει, ἐν ψύχει καὶ γυμνότητι, ἐν διωγμοῖς καὶ στενοχωρίαις, ἐφ' οἷς ἄλλοι δυσανασχετοῦσι καὶ πρὸς τὸν βίον ἀπαγορεύουσιν, ἐπὶ τού τοις αὐτὸς ἀγαλλιώμενος. Οἱ τοίνυν ἀπαιδεύτως ἔχοντες τῆς ἀποστολικῆς διανοίας, καὶ μὴ συνιέντες, ὅτι πρὸς τὴν εὐαγγελικὴν ἡμᾶς προσκαλεῖται ζωὴν, τολμῶσι κατηγορεῖν τοῦ Παύλου, ὡς ἀδύνατα ἡμῖν διορίζοντος. Ἀλλὰ μὴν διδασκέσθωσαν ὅσαι τοῦ χαίρειν εὐλόγως αἱ ἀφορμαὶ διὰ τῆς τοῦ Θεοῦ μεγαλοδωρεᾶς ἡμῖν πρόκεινται. Παρήχθημεν εἰς τὸ εἶναι, μὴ ὄντες· κατ' εἰκόνα τοῦ κτίσαντος ἐγενήθημεν· νοῦν καὶ λόγον συμπληροῦντα ἡμῶν τὴν φύσιν ἔχομεν, δι' οὗ Θεὸν ἐγνωρίσαμεν. Καὶ τὰ κάλλη τῆς κτίσεως ἐν τέχνως καταμανθάνοντες, δι' αὐτῶν, οἱονεὶ διὰ γραμ μάτων τινῶν, τὴν μεγάλην τοῦ Θεοῦ περὶ πάντα πρόνοιαν καὶ σοφίαν ἀναγινώσκομεν. Διακριτικοί ἐσμεν ἀγαθοῦ καὶ τοῦ χείρονος· ἐκλογὴν τοῦ συμφέροντος καὶ ἀποστροφὴν τοῦ βλαβεροῦ ἐξ αὐτῆς τῆς φύσεως δεδιδάγμεθα. Ἀλλοτριωθέντες Θεοῦ διὰ τῆς ἁμαρτίας, πάλιν εἰς τὴν οἰκειότητα ἀνεκλήθημεν, τῷ αἵματι τοῦ Μονογενοῦς ἐκ τῆς ἀτίμου δουλείας ἐξαιρεθέντες. Ἀναστάσεως ἐλπίδες, ἀγγελικῶν ἀγα θῶν ἀπολαύσεις, ἡ ἐν οὐρανοῖς βασιλεία, τὰ ἐν ἐπαγγελίαις ἀγαθὰ, καὶ διανοίας καὶ λόγου δύναμιν ὑπερ βαίνοντα.
thought_title: The Apostle's high aim and the soul's unshaken joy
orientation: Basil is answering the objectors who called Paul's command to rejoice always impossible, by explaining that Paul addresses the spiritually minded, not those living by the flesh.
pass_a_gloss: What then do we say? That, while the Apostle looks toward other things, and tries to lift our souls from the ground toward height, and to transfer them to the heavenly citizenship, those who do not reach the greatness of mind of the lawgiver, crawling around earth and flesh, like worms around a mire, in the sufferings of the body, demand the possibility of the apostolic ordinances. But he summons to rejoice always not the ordinary person, but the one such as he himself was, no longer living in flesh, but having Christ living in himself, since the union with the highest of goods in no way admits the sympathy from the troublesome things of the flesh. But even if the flesh is cut, the dissolution of continuity remains in the part of the body that suffered, since the transmission of what grieves is not able to reach through to the intellectual part of the soul. For if we put to death the members that are on the earth, according to the instructions of the Apostle, and carried about the dying of Jesus in the body, necessarily the blow from the deadened body will not make its way to the soul that has been released from its union with it. And dishonors and losses and deaths of relatives will not go up to the mind, nor will they turn down the height of the soul toward the sympathy here. For if those who have fallen into difficulties think the same things as the earnest person, they will not provide griefs to another, since they themselves do not bear what befalls them grievously; but if they live according to the flesh, not even so will they grieve, but they will be judged pitiable, more because they do not choose what is needful than because of their circumstances. And in general a soul that has once been bound to the longing for the Creator, and has become accustomed to be brightened by the beauties there, will not change its exceeding joy and cheerfulness because of the varied change of fleshly sufferings; but it will make for itself the things grievous to others an increase of gladness. Such was the Apostle, taking pleasure in weaknesses, in afflictions, in persecutions, in necessities, making his wants his boasts; in famine and thirst, in cold and nakedness, in persecutions and distresses, at which others are impatient and renounce life, at these things he himself rejoicing. Those therefore who are uninstructed in the apostolic mind, and do not understand that he summons us to the gospel life, dare to accuse Paul, as one who prescribes impossible things for us. But indeed let them be taught how many occasions for rejoicing reasonably lie before us through the great gift of God. We were brought into being, not having been; we were made according to the image of the Creator; we have mind and reason completing our nature, through which we have come to know God. And learning the beauties of creation skillfully, through them, as through certain letters, we read the great providence and wisdom of God concerning all things. We are able to distinguish good from the worse; we have been taught from nature itself the choice of what is beneficial and the avoidance of what is harmful. Having been alienated from God through sin, we were called back again to kinship, having been rescued from dishonorable slavery by the blood of the Only-begotten. Hopes of resurrection, enjoyments of angelic goods, the kingdom in the heavens, the good things in the promises, surpassing the power of both mind and reason.

choices.why: The glossary requires 'citizenship' for πολίτευμα, referring to the heavenly commonwealth to which Paul summons believers.
The glossary requires 'sufferings' for πάθη, the natural affections of the body that must be kept within limits.

choices.english: the intellectual part of the soul
choices.why: Renders the contrast between the bodily part that suffers and the rational, intellectual faculty of the soul that remains untouched.

choices.term: τὰ μέλη τὰ ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς
choices.english: the members that are on the earth
choices.why: Echoes Colossians 3:5 wording, keeping the literal spatial phrase 'on the earth' to preserve the Pauline allusion.
Echoes 2 Corinthians 4:10 wording; 'dying' preserves the process sense of νέκρωσις rather than the state 'death.'

choices.english: will make for itself an increase of gladness
choices.why: The middle voice ποιήσεται means the soul actively makes griefs into an increase of gladness for itself, not that they passively become one.
rejected: will become an increase of gladness
will be made an increase of gladness

pass_b_english: What do we say, then? The Apostle is looking toward other things and trying to lift our souls from the ground to the height and transfer them to the heavenly citizenship. But those who do not reach the lawgiver's greatness of mind crawl around earth and flesh like worms in the mire, in the body's passions, and demand that the apostolic ordinances be possible on their own terms. Yet he summons to rejoice always not just anyone, but the kind of person he himself was: no longer living in the flesh, but having Christ living in himself, so that the union with the highest of goods in no way admits the sympathy that comes from the body's troubles. Even if the flesh is cut, the breaking of its continuity remains in the part of the body that suffered, because the spread of what grieves cannot reach through to the intellectual part of the soul. For if we have put to death the members that are on the earth, according to the Apostle's instructions, and we carry about the deadness of Jesus in the body (2 Corinthians 4:10), then necessarily the blow from the body that has been put to death will not reach to the soul that has been released from its connection to it. Dishonors and losses and the deaths of loved ones will not rise up to the mind, nor will they turn the soul's height down toward sympathy with things here. For if those who have fallen into difficulties think the same way as the earnest person, they will not cause grief to another, since they themselves do not bear what happens in a grieving way. But if they live according to the flesh, they will not cause grief even so; rather, they will be judged pitiable, not so much because of their circumstances as because they do not choose what is right. In general, a soul that has once been bound to the longing for its Creator and has become accustomed to being brightened by the beauties there will not have its exceeding gladness and cheerfulness changed by the varied shifting of the body's sufferings. Instead, it will make for itself an increase of gladness out of the things that grieve others. Such was the Apostle, taking pleasure in weaknesses, in afflictions, in persecutions, in necessities, making his wants his boasts: in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness, in persecutions and distresses—the very things at which others are indignant and give up on life, in these he was exulting. Those, then, who are untrained in the apostolic mind and do not understand that he is summoning us to the gospel life dare to accuse Paul of prescribing impossible things for us. But let them be taught how many reasonable grounds for rejoicing are set before us through God's great gift. We were brought into being when we did not exist. We were made according to the image of our Creator. We have mind and reason completing our nature, through which we have come to know God. And as we study with skill the beauties of creation, through them, as through certain letters, we read God's great providence and wisdom over all things. We are able to distinguish good from evil. We have been taught by nature itself to choose what is beneficial and turn away from what is harmful. Having been alienated from God through sin, we were called back again to kinship with him, rescued from dishonorable slavery by the blood of the Only-Begotten. There are hopes of resurrection, enjoyments of angelic goods, the kingdom in the heavens, the good things promised, surpassing the power of mind and reason.

problems.why: "νέκρωσις" means "putting to death/deadness," not "dying" (process). Paul carries death, not a dying process.
"χωρήσει" means "will not reach/penetrate," not "make its way." The blow doesn't travel to the soul.

problems.quote: they will not cause grief even so
problems.why: Misread: "they will not grieve [others] even so" is wrong. The sense is "even so they will not grieve [the saint]," or "they won't be a cause of grief." But contextually, the point is that fleshly people don't make the spiritual person grieve.
problems.fix: they will not grieve him even so

problems.quote: more because they do not choose what is right than because of their circumstances
problems.source_quote: οὐ τῶν περιστάσεων μᾶλλον, ἢ τοῦ μὴ προαιρεῖσθαι τὰ δέοντα
problems.why: Reversed comparison: "not more because of circumstances than because of not choosing what is right" means circumstances are NOT the main reason; their failure to choose rightly IS. English says opposite.
problems.fix: not so much because of their circumstances as because they do not choose what is right

problems.why: "περιχαρές" means "exceeding joy/very gladness," not "overflowing joy and good cheer." "εὔθυμον" is "cheerfulness/good spirits."
"χείρονος" means "the worse/evil," not "what is worse" in comparative sense. "Good from evil" is the standard contrast.

problems.quote: the good things in the promises that surpass the power of mind and reason
problems.source_quote: τὰ ἐν ἐπαγγελίαις ἀγαθὰ, καὶ διανοίας καὶ λόγου δύναμιν ὑπερβαίνοντα
problems.why: Syntactic error: "τὰ ἐν ἐπαγγελίαις ἀγαθά" is one item, "ἀναστάσεως ἐλπίδες" etc. are all subjects. The final phrase modifies the promised goods: "surpassing mind and reason's power." English makes "mind and reason" separate from the list.
problems.fix: the good things promised, surpassing the power of mind and reason
problems.ruling: διανοίας καὶ λόγου δύναμιν ὑπερβαίνοντα modifies τὰ ἐν ἐπαγγελίαις ἀγαθά, not a separate item; English obscures syntax.

fixed: the dying of Jesus: νέκρωσις means deadness/putting to death, not the process of dying.
will not make its way: χωρήσει means will not reach/penetrate.
they will not cause grief even so: the fleshly people do not grieve the saint; they will not grieve him even so.
more because they do not choose what is right than because of their circumstances: comparison reversed; circumstances are not the main reason, their failure to choose rightly is.
overflowing joy and good cheer: περιχαρές is exceeding gladness, εὔθυμον is cheerfulness.
what is worse: χείρονος means evil, not a comparative.
the good things in the promises that surpass the power of mind and reason: the final phrase modifies the promised goods, not mind and reason as separate items.

problems.quote: they will not grieve him even so
problems.why: Subject is unclear; "they" refers to the sufferers, but "him" is wrong—no masculine singular object in source. Means "they will not cause grief" generally.
problems.fix: they will not cause grief even so
problems.ruling: οὐδ' οὕτω λυπήσουσιν has no masculine singular object; 'him' invents one, misleading the reader about syntax and referent.

edits.old: they will not grieve him even so
edits.new: they will not cause grief even so

fixed: Changed 'they will not grieve him even so' to 'they will not cause grief even so': the source 'οὐδ' οὕτω λυπήσουσιν' has no masculine singular object, and the verb λυπέω here means to cause grief generally, not to grieve a specific person.

problems.why: "πάθεσι" here means affections/passions, not sufferings; the metaphor is about being stuck in bodily passions, not suffering.
problems.ruling: πάθεσι here = passions/affections, not sufferings; worms in mire metaphor targets bodily passions, not pain.

fixed: Changed 'in the body's sufferings' to 'in the body's passions' because πάθεσι here refers to affections/passions, not sufferings.

dismissed.quote: the intellectual part of the soul
dismissed.why: 'Intellectual' suggests discursive reason; νοερόν here means the soul's higher, spiritual/intelligent faculty, its 'mind' or 'noetic' part.
dismissed.note: 'The intellectual part of the soul' is a standard rendering of τὸ νοερόν, and 'the mind of the soul' would be clumsier.
